{{short description|Type of space in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[algebraic geometry]], a '''formal scheme''' is a type of space which includes data about its surroundings. Unlike an ordinary [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]], a formal scheme includes infinitesimal data that, in effect, points in a direction off of the scheme. For this reason, formal schemes frequently appear in topics such as [[deformation theory]]. But the concept is also used to prove a theorem such as the [[theorem on formal functions]], which is used to deduce theorems of interest for usual schemes.

A locally Noetherian scheme is a locally Noetherian formal scheme in the canonical way: the formal completion along itself. In other words, the category of locally Noetherian formal schemes contains all locally Noetherian schemes.

Formal schemes were motivated by and generalize [[Oscar Zariski|Zariski]]'s theory of [[formal holomorphic function]]s.

Algebraic geometry based on formal schemes is called '''formal algebraic geometry'''.

== Definition ==
Formal schemes are usually defined only in the [[Noetherian scheme|Noetherian]] case. While there have been several definitions of non-Noetherian formal schemes, these encounter technical problems. Consequently, we will only define locally Noetherian formal schemes.

All rings will be assumed to be [[commutative ring|commutative]] and with [[unital ring|unit]]. Let ''A'' be a (Noetherian) [[topological ring]], that is, a ring ''A'' which is a [[topological space]] such that the operations of addition and multiplication are continuous. ''A'' is '''[[linear topology|linearly topologized]]''' if zero has a [[base (topology)|base]] consisting of [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]]s. An '''ideal of definition''' <math>\mathcal{J}</math> for a linearly topologized ring is an open ideal such that for every open neighborhood ''V'' of 0, there exists a positive integer ''n'' such that <math>\mathcal{J}^n \subseteq V</math>. A linearly topologized ring is '''preadmissible''' if it admits an ideal of definition, and it is '''admissible''' if it is also [[completion (ring theory)|complete]]. (In the terminology of [[Nicolas Bourbaki|Bourbaki]], this is "complete and separated".)

Assume that ''A'' is admissible, and let <math>\mathcal{J}</math> be an ideal of definition. A prime ideal is open if and only if it contains <math>\mathcal{J}</math>. The set of open prime ideals of ''A'', or equivalently the set of prime ideals of <math>A/\mathcal{J}</math>, is the underlying topological space of the '''formal spectrum''' of ''A'', denoted Spf ''A''. Spf ''A'' has a [[structure sheaf]] which is defined using the structure sheaf of the [[spectrum of a ring]]. Let <math>\mathcal{J}_\lambda</math> be a neighborhood basis for zero consisting of ideals of definition. All the spectra of <math>A/\mathcal{J}_\lambda</math> have the same underlying topological space but a different structure sheaf. The structure sheaf of Spf ''A'' is the [[projective limit]] <math>\varprojlim_\lambda \mathcal{O}_{\text{Spec} A/\mathcal{J}_\lambda}</math>.

It can be shown that if ''f'' &isin; ''A'' and ''D''<sub>''f''</sub> is the set of all open prime ideals of ''A'' not containing ''f'', then <math>\mathcal{O}_{\text{Spf} A}(D_f) = \widehat{A_f}</math>, where <math>\widehat{A_f}</math> is the completion of the [[localization of a ring|localization]] ''A''<sub>''f''</sub>.

Finally, a '''locally Noetherian formal scheme''' is a topologically ringed space <math>(\mathfrak{X}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}})</math> (that is, a [[ringed space]] whose sheaf of rings is a sheaf of topological rings) such that each point of <math>\mathfrak{X}</math> admits an open neighborhood isomorphic (as topologically ringed spaces) to the formal spectrum of a Noetherian ring.

== Morphisms between formal schemes ==
A morphism <math>f: \mathfrak{X} \to \mathfrak{Y}</math> of locally Noetherian formal schemes is a morphism of them as locally ringed spaces such that the induced map <math>f^{\#}: \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}_\mathfrak{Y}) \to \Gamma(f^{-1}(U), \mathcal{O}_\mathfrak{X})</math> is a continuous homomorphism of topological rings for any affine open subset ''U''.

''f'' is said to be ''adic'' or ''<math>\mathfrak{X}</math> is a <math>\mathfrak{Y}</math>-adic formal scheme'' if there exists an ideal of definition <math>\mathcal{I}</math> such that <math>f^*(\mathcal{I}) \mathcal{O}_\mathfrak{X}</math> is an ideal of definition for <math>\mathfrak{X}</math>. If ''f'' is adic, then this property holds for any ideal of definition.

== Examples ==

For any ideal <math>I</math> and ring <math>A</math> we can define the [[I-adic topology|''<math>I</math>-adic topology'']] on <math>A</math>, defined by its basis consisting of sets of the form <math>a+I^n</math>. This is preadmissible, and admissible if <math>A</math> is <math>I</math>-adically complete. In this case <math>\operatorname{Spf} A</math> is the topological space <math>\operatorname{Spec} A/I</math> with sheaf of rings <math>\lim_n \mathcal{O}_{\text{Spec} A/I^n}=\lim_n \widetilde{A/I^n}</math> instead of <math>\widetilde{A/I}</math>.

# <math>A = k [ \! [ t ] \! ]</math> and <math>I = (t)</math>. Then <math>A/I = k</math> so the space <math>\operatorname{Spf} A</math> a single point <math>(t)</math> on which its structure sheaf takes value <math>k [ \! [ t ] \! ]</math>. Compare this to <math>\operatorname{Spec} A/I</math>, whose structure sheaf takes value <math>k</math> at this point: this is an example of the idea that <math>\operatorname{Spf} A</math> is a 'formal thickening' of <math>A</math> about <math>I</math>.
# The formal completion of a closed subscheme. Consider the closed subscheme <math>X</math> of the affine plane over <math>k</math>, defined by the ideal <math>I = (y^2 - x^3)</math>. Note that <math>A_0 = k[x,y]</math> is not <math>I</math>-adically complete; write <math>A</math> for its <math>I</math>-adic completion. In this case, <math>\operatorname{Spf} A = X</math> as spaces and its structure sheaf is <math>\lim_n \widetilde{k[x,y]/I^n}</math>. Its global sections are <math>A</math>, as opposed to <math>X</math> whose global sections are <math>A/I</math>.
